subject: Immunology
topic: SCID IL-2RG Common Gamma Chain vs Adenosine Deaminase Deficiency
stem: A 3-month-old male infant presents with chronic candidal diaper dermatitis, persistent oral thrush, intractable watery diarrhea with failure to thrive, and severe Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia. Complete blood count reveals severe lymphopenia with an absolute lymphocyte count of 420/uL (normal > 3,000/uL). Flow cytometry demonstrates absent T cells (CD3+ < 1%) and absent natural killer cells (CD16+/CD56+ < 1%), but normal or elevated numbers of immature B cells (CD19+ 92%). Serum IgG, IgA, and IgM levels are all profoundly diminished. Chest radiography confirms the complete absence of a thymic shadow. Which of the following molecular defects accounts for this patient's T(-) B(+) NK(-) severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID)?

options.text: X-linked mutation in the IL2RG gene encoding the common gamma chain shared by interleukin receptors
options.explanation: X-LINKED SEVERE COMBINED IMMUNODEFICIENCY (X-SCID) accounts for approx. 50% of all SCID cases and is caused by pathogenic mutations in the IL2RG gene on chromosome Xq13.1. This gene encodes the COMMON GAMMA CHAIN (gamma-c, CD132) shared by cytokine receptors for IL-2, IL-4, IL-7, IL-9, IL-15, and IL-21. Defective IL-7 signaling halts thymic T-cell differentiation (causing profound T-cell absence and absent thymic shadow), while defective IL-15 signaling prevents natural killer (NK) cell development. B cells are present in normal numbers (T- B+ NK- phenotype) because early B-cell ontogeny does not require the common gamma chain, but B cells are functionally inert and cannot produce antibodies due to the lack of T-cell help. In contrast, ADENOSINE DEAMINASE (ADA) deficiency causes T(-) B(-) NK(-) SCID due to toxic dATP accumulation in all lymphocytes.

options.text: Autosomal recessive deficiency of adenosine deaminase causing intracellular accumulation of deoxyadenosine
options.explanation: Adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency causes autosomal recessive SCID with a T(-) B(-) NK(-) phenotype because toxic dATP accumulation causes apoptosis in all lymphocyte lineages, including B cells.

options.text: Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) mutation arresting B-cell differentiation at the pre-B stage
options.explanation: BTK deficiency causes X-linked agammaglobulinemia, characterized by absent B cells (CD19/CD20 = 0) with completely normal T-cell and NK-cell numbers.

options.text: Microdeletion of chromosome 22q11.2 causing failure of third and fourth pharyngeal pouch development
options.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion) causes thymic hypoplasia with variable T-cell deficiency, but B cells and NK cells are normal, and patients typically exhibit hypocalcemia and conotruncal cardiac anomalies.

options.text: Mutation in the RAG1 or RAG2 genes impairing V(D)J somatic recombination in antigen receptors
options.explanation: RAG1/RAG2 mutations cause autosomal recessive SCID with a T(-) B(-) NK(+) phenotype, as V(D)J recombination is required for both T-cell receptors and B-cell immunoglobulins, but not NK cells.

subject: Immunology
topic: X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia Bruton Tyrosine Kinase Pre-B Cell Arrest
stem: A 9-month-old male infant presents with his third episode of acute otitis media and second episode of lobar Streptococcus pneumoniae pneumonia in the past 4 months. He was healthy until 6 months of age, when recurrent sinopulmonary bacterial infections began. Physical examination reveals absent pharyngeal lymphoid tissue (scanty, nearly invisible tonsils) and no palpable cervical lymph nodes despite active purulent bacterial infection. Serum immunoglobulin quantification reveals: IgG 45 mg/dL (normal 300-1,000 mg/dL), IgA < 5 mg/dL, and IgM 12 mg/dL. Peripheral blood flow cytometry demonstrates completely normal numbers of mature CD3+ T lymphocytes and CD16+/CD56+ NK cells, but CD19+ and CD20+ B lymphocytes are virtually undetectable (< 0.1%). Which of the following cellular developmental stages is arrested in this patient's bone marrow?

options.text: Pro-B cell stage due to failure of immunoglobulin heavy-chain D-to-J gene segment rearrangement
options.explanation: Heavy-chain D-to-J rearrangement occurs in early pro-B cells and requires RAG1/RAG2 recombinases; BTK acts downstream at the pre-B stage after heavy-chain assembly.

options.text: Pre-B cell stage due to failure of light-chain gene rearrangement mediated by Bruton tyrosine kinase
options.explanation: X-LINKED AGAMMAGLOBULINEMIA (XLA / BRUTON AGAMMAGLOBULINEMIA) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the BTK gene on chromosome Xq22.1, which encodes BRUTON TYROSINE KINASE, a non-receptor cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase. In bone marrow B-cell lymphopoiesis, pre-B cell receptor signaling via BTK is essential for survival, allelic exclusion, and transition from the PRE-B CELL STAGE (heavy chain rearranged and expressed with surrogate light chains) to the IMMATURE B CELL STAGE (rearrangement of kappa/lambda light chains). Defective BTK causes complete maturation arrest at the pre-B stage, leading to apoptotic clearance in the marrow. Consequently, NO MATURE B CELLS (CD19-/CD20-) enter peripheral blood, secondary lymphoid organs lack germinal centers (hypoplastic tonsils, absent lymph nodes), and all immunoglobulin isotypes are profoundly depleted after maternal IgG wanes at 6 months.

options.text: Mature naive B-cell stage due to failure of CD40-mediated class-switch recombination in lymph nodes
options.explanation: Arrest at the mature naive B-cell stage occurs in Hyper-IgM syndrome (CD40L defect), where B-cell numbers are normal but class-switching fails.

options.text: Plasmablast stage due to impaired somatic hypermutation mediated by activation-induced cytidine deaminase
options.explanation: Defects in activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID) prevent somatic hypermutation and class-switching, causing autosomal recessive Hyper-IgM syndrome with normal B-cell counts.

options.text: Common lymphoid progenitor stage due to failure of IL-7 receptor alpha-chain signaling cascades
options.explanation: Common lymphoid progenitor failure impairs both T and B cell lineage development, producing SCID rather than isolated B-cell deficiency.

subject: Immunology
topic: Hyper-IgM Syndrome CD40L Defect and Class-Switch Recombination Failure
stem: A 10-month-old male infant presents with persistent fever, tachypnea, and diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates. Bronchoalveolar lavage demonstrates cyst walls of Pneumocystis jirovecii on methenamine silver staining. He also has a history of recurrent severe Cryptosporidium parvum watery diarrhea and recurrent otitis media. Physical examination reveals normal pharyngeal tonsils and palpable cervical lymph nodes. Complete blood count shows absolute neutrophil count of 450/uL (severe neutropenia), normal absolute lymphocyte count, and normal numbers of circulating CD19+ B lymphocytes. Immunoglobulin quantification demonstrates: serum IgM markedly elevated at 480 mg/dL (normal 40-140 mg/dL), serum IgG profoundly decreased at 38 mg/dL, and serum IgA undetectable. Flow cytometry demonstrates absent expression of CD154 on activated helper T cells. Which of the following molecular interactions is disrupted in this patient?

options.text: Interaction between B7-1/B7-2 (CD80/CD86) on antigen-presenting cells and CD28 on naive T cells
options.explanation: B7-CD28 interaction provides essential costimulation for naive T-cell activation; blockade impairs general T-cell activation without the isolated Hyper-IgM phenotype.

options.text: Binding of programmed death ligand-1 (PD-L1) to PD-1 on exhausted cytotoxic T lymphocytes
options.explanation: PD-1/PD-L1 is an inhibitory checkpoint pathway involved in immune tolerance and tumor evasion, not B-cell class-switch recombination.

options.text: Engagement of CD40 on B cells and macrophages by CD40L (CD154) on activated CD4+ T helper cells
options.explanation: X-LINKED HYPER-IgM SYNDROME is caused by mutations in the CD40LG gene on the X chromosome, which encodes CD40 LIGAND (CD40L / CD154), a transmembrane protein expressed on activated CD4+ T helper cells. CD40L binds constitutively expressed CD40 on B cells, dendritic cells, and macrophages. In B cells, CD40-CD40L costimulation activates NF-kappa-B and upregulates ACTIVATION-INDUCED CYTIDINE DEAMINASE (AID), driving IMMUNOGLOBULIN CLASS-SWITCH RECOMBINATION (from IgM/IgD to IgG, IgA, and IgE) and somatic hypermutation. Without CD40L, B cells secrete only IgM (normal/elevated IgM, profoundly low IgG/IgA/IgE). In macrophages, lack of CD40L engagement prevents macrophage activation and cytokine production, severely impairing CELL-MEDIATED IMMUNITY and predisposing to opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis jirovecii, Cryptosporidium) and chronic neutropenia.

options.text: Engagement of fas ligand (CD178) with fas receptor (CD95) during lymphocyte apoptosis
options.explanation: Fas-FasL mutations cause Autoimmune Lymphoproliferative Syndrome (ALPS), characterized by non-malignant lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, and double-negative (CD4- CD8-) T cells.

options.text: Interaction of LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18) with intercellular adhesion molecule-1 (ICAM-1)
options.explanation: LFA-1/ICAM-1 mediates leukocyte adhesion and extravasation; mutations cause Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type 1, presenting with delayed umbilical cord separation and neutrophilia.

subject: Immunology
topic: Common Variable Immunodeficiency Defective Plasma Cell Differentiation
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents with a 4-year history of recurrent bacterial sinopulmonary infections (recurrent Streptococcus pneumoniae and Haemophilus influenzae sinusitis and bronchitis), chronic diarrhea with Giardia lamblia cysts in stool, and persistent fatigue. High-resolution chest CT demonstrates bilateral cylindrical bronchiectasis in the lower lobes. Abdominal examination reveals splenomegaly. Serum immunoglobulin quantification reveals: IgG 160 mg/dL (normal 700-1,600 mg/dL), IgA 18 mg/dL (normal 70-400 mg/dL), and IgM 24 mg/dL (normal 40-230 mg/dL). Isohemagglutinin titers are undetectable, and she fails to mount specific antibody responses following immunization with tetanus toxoid and 23-valent pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccines. Peripheral blood flow cytometry demonstrates completely normal numbers of circulating CD19+ B lymphocytes and CD3+ T lymphocytes. Which of the following immunopathological mechanisms is the hallmark of this condition?

options.text: Premature apoptosis of common lymphoid progenitors in the fetal liver and bone marrow
options.explanation: Apoptosis of common lymphoid progenitors causes SCID, with severe lymphopenia affecting both T and B lineages, presenting in early infancy.

options.text: Complete failure of thymic epithelial stroma to support negative selection of autoreactive T cells
options.explanation: Thymic selection failure causes autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy (APECED / APS-1 due to AIRE mutations), not hypogammaglobulinemia.

options.text: Selective deletion of immunoglobulin heavy chain constant region gamma genes on chromosome 14
options.explanation: Specific constant region deletions cause isolated subclass deficiencies, not pan-hypogammaglobulinemia involving IgG, IgA, and IgM.

options.text: Impaired terminal differentiation of mature B cells into immunoglobulin-secreting plasma cells
options.explanation: COMMON VARIABLE IMMUNODEFICIENCY (CVID) is the most common clinically significant primary antibody deficiency disorder diagnosed in young adults. The fundamental immunopathogenesis is HETEROGENEOUS DEFECTIVE TERMINAL DIFFERENTIATION OF MATURE B CELLS INTO PLASMA CELLS. In contrast to XLA (where B cells are absent), patients with CVID have NORMAL OR NEAR-NORMAL NUMBERS OF CIRCULATING B CELLS (CD19+/CD20+), but these B cells fail to differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells and switched memory B cells. This leads to marked hypogammaglobulinemia (typically IgG > 2 SD below mean plus low IgA and/or IgM) and absent vaccine antibody responses. Clinical features include recurrent sinopulmonary infections, bronchiectasis, Giardia enteritis, autoimmune cytopenias, splenomegaly, and non-caseating granulomatous disease.

options.text: Inability of follicular dendritic cells to capture antigen-complement complexes via CR1/CR2 receptors
options.explanation: While FDC trapping assists affinity maturation, CVID is driven by intrinsic B-cell and T-follicular helper signaling defects (e.g., TACI, ICOS, CD19 mutations) blocking plasma cell maturation.

subject: Immunology
topic: Selective IgA Deficiency Mucosal Immunity and Anaphylaxis to Blood Products
stem: A 22-year-old woman with a history of recurrent mild sinopulmonary infections, allergic rhinitis, and celiac disease undergoes an urgent packed red blood cell transfusion following traumatic blood loss in a motor vehicle collision. Within 3 minutes of initiating the transfusion, she abruptly develops severe dyspnea, wheezing, diffuse urticaria, facial angioedema, and profound hypotension with blood pressure dropping to 72/40 mm Hg. The blood unit is cross-match compatible (O negative donor to O negative recipient) and shows no signs of hemolysis, bacterial contamination, or clerical mismatch. Serum immunoglobulin quantification performed after acute stabilization reveals: serum IgA < 1.0 mg/dL (normal 70-400 mg/dL), with completely normal serum IgG (1,150 mg/dL) and normal serum IgM (140 mg/dL). High-titer anti-IgA antibodies of the IgE isotype are detected in the patient's serum. Which of the following immunological mechanisms accounts for her life-threatening transfusion reaction?

options.text: Pre-formed anti-HLA class I antibodies activating donor complement via the classical pathway
options.explanation: Anti-HLA antibodies cause febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reactions (FNHTR) or Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury (TRALI), not immediate IgA-mediated anaphylactic shock.

options.text: Recipient ABO isohemagglutinins binding donor erythrocyte carbohydrates provoking intravascular hemolysis
options.explanation: ABO mismatch causes acute hemolytic transfusion reaction (fever, flank pain, hemoglobinuria, DIC), but the blood was cross-match compatible O-negative to O-negative.

options.text: Donor anti-leukocyte antibodies binding recipient pulmonary capillary endothelium
options.explanation: Donor anti-leukocyte antibodies causing pulmonary capillary leak is the mechanism of TRALI, presenting with non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema without diffuse urticaria or anti-IgA antibodies.

options.text: Passive transfer of donor IgE antibodies against dietary peanut allergens in donor plasma
options.explanation: Passive transfer of donor food allergies can occasionally occur, but the presence of recipient anti-IgA antibodies proves recipient sensitization to donor IgA.

options.text: Pre-formed anti-IgA IgE antibodies cross-link Fc-epsilon-RI receptors on mast cells upon exposure to donor plasma IgA
options.explanation: SELECTIVE IgA DEFICIENCY is the most common primary immunodeficiency (prevalence ~1:600). Patients have profoundly low or undetectable serum and secretory IgA with normal IgG and IgM. Because these patients have never been exposed to endogenous IgA, the immune system views foreign IgA as an exogenous antigen. Up to 40% of patients with absolute IgA deficiency produce CLASS-SWITCHED ANTI-IgA ANTIBODIES (predominantly IgG or IgE). When exposed to donor blood products (RBCs, platelets, plasma) containing even minute traces of donor IgA, recipient anti-IgA IgE antibodies cross-link FC-EPSILON-RI RECEPTORS on mast cells and basophils, triggering immediate degranulation, histamine and leukotriene release, and life-threatening ANAPHYLAXIS. Such patients require washed RBCs or blood products from IgA-deficient donors.

subject: Immunology
topic: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome WASp Actin Cytoskeleton and Microthrombocytopenia
stem: A 14-month-old boy presents with bleeding following routine circumcised wound care, recurrent petechiae, severe flexural atopic eczema, and recurrent encapsulated bacterial sinopulmonary infections. Complete blood count reveals: hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, white blood cell count 8,200/uL, and platelet count 28,000/uL (normal 150,000-450,000/uL). Peripheral blood smear confirms severe thrombocytopenia with strikingly SMALL, ATROPHIC PLATELETS (mean platelet volume 5.8 fL, normal 7.5-11.5 fL). Serum immunoglobulin profiling demonstrates low IgM, elevated IgA, and markedly elevated IgE. Genetic analysis confirms an X-linked mutation in the WAS gene. Which of the following cellular processes is directly dependent on the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp) and fails in this disorder?

options.text: Relaying intracellular signals from cell-surface receptors to Arp2/3-mediated actin cytoskeleton remodeling
options.explanation: WISKOTT-ALDRICH SYNDROME (WAS) is an X-LINKED RECESSIVE disorder caused by mutations in the WAS gene, which encodes the Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASp). WASp is expressed exclusively in hematopoietic cells and functions as a molecular bridge linking small Rho-family GTPases (Cdc42 and Rac) to the ARP2/3 COMPLEX. Arp2/3 nucleates branched ACTIN FILAMENT POLYMERIZATION, which is required for: (1) Megakaryocyte proplatelet formation and platelet budding (causing MICROTHROMBOCYTOPENIA with abnormally small platelets, the pathognomonic finding); (2) T-cell immunological synapse formation and receptor capping; and (3) Leukocyte chemotaxis, adhesion, and phagocytosis. Patients present with the classic triad: THROMBOCYTOPENIA WITH SMALL PLATELETS, ECZEMA, and RECURRENT INFECTIONS, with characteristic low IgM and high IgA/IgE.

options.text: Targeting lysosomal hydrolases to the inner membrane through mannose-6-phosphate tagging
options.explanation: Mannose-6-phosphate tagging failure is the mechanism of I-cell disease (mucolipidosis II), causing coarse facial features, skeletal abnormalities, and elevated plasma lysosomal enzymes.

options.text: Assembly of the NADPH oxidase multi-protein complex in phagolysosomal membranes
options.explanation: NADPH oxidase failure causes Chronic Granulomatous Disease, characterized by recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms without microthrombocytopenia or eczema.

options.text: Translocation of cytoplasmic NF-kappa-B into the nucleus following I-kappa-B phosphorylation
options.explanation: NF-kappa-B essential modulator (NEMO / IKK-gamma) mutations cause anhidrotic ectodermal dysplasia with immunodeficiency, not microthrombocytopenia.

options.text: DNA double-strand break repair through homologous recombination and non-homologous end-joining
options.explanation: DNA double-strand break repair failure causes Ataxia-Telangiectasia (ATM mutation) or Nijmegen breakage syndrome, characterized by cerebellar ataxia and oculocutaneous telangiectasias.

subject: Genetics
topic: Ataxia-Telangiectasia ATM Kinase and DNA Double-Strand Break Repair Failure
stem: A 4-year-old girl is evaluated for progressive clumsiness and frequent falls. Neurological examination reveals marked truncal and gait ataxia, horizontal nystagmus, dysmetria, and slurred speech. Physical examination reveals fine, branching, prominent capillary dilations on her bulbar conjunctivae and pinnae (oculocutaneous telangiectasias). She has a history of multiple recurrent episodes of sinus and bacterial lung infections requiring hospitalization. Laboratory evaluation reveals marked elevation of serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP 148 ng/mL, normal < 10 ng/mL) and deficiency of IgA and IgG2. Cultured patient fibroblasts demonstrate extreme hypersensitivity to ionizing radiation, with frequent non-homologous chromosomal translocations involving chromosomes 7 and 14. Which of the following molecular functions is carried out by the protein mutated in this autosomal recessive disorder?

options.text: DNA helicase unwinding damaged DNA during nucleotide excision repair of pyrimidine dimers
options.explanation: Nucleotide excision repair defects cause Xeroderma Pigmentosum, characterized by extreme ultraviolet (UV) sensitivity, skin freckling, and skin cancers, not cerebellar ataxia.

options.text: Serine/threonine kinase that senses DNA double-strand breaks and coordinates p53 cell-cycle arrest
options.explanation: ATAXIA-TELANGIECTASIA is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative immunodeficiency caused by mutations in the ATM GENE on chromosome 11q22.3. The ATM protein is a master SERINE/THREONINE PROTEIN KINASE belonging to the PI3K-related kinase (PIKK) family. When DNA DOUBLE-STRAND BREAKS (DSBs) occur (e.g., from ionizing radiation, free radicals, or physiological V(D)J recombination), ATM senses the breaks and rapidly phosphorylates key downstream substrates, including p53 (Ser15), Chk2, and BRCA1. This activates G1/S and G2/M CELL-CYCLE CHECKPOINTS and initiates homologous recombination or non-homologous end-joining (NHEJ). ATM deficiency leads to defective DNA repair, neurodegeneration (PURKINJE CELL ATROPHY -> cerebellar ataxia), OCULOCUTANEOUS TELANGIECTASIAS, MARKEDLY ELEVATED ALPHA-FETOPROTEIN (AFP), IgA deficiency, extreme IONIZING RADIATION SENSITIVITY, and high risk of hematologic malignancies.

options.text: DNA mismatch repair endonuclease recognizing base-base mismatches and insertion-deletion loops
options.explanation: Mismatch repair defects (MSH2, MLH1) cause Lynch syndrome (hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer) with microsatellite instability.

options.text: Transcriptional transactivator mediating negative selection of autoreactive thymocytes
options.explanation: Autoimmune regulator (AIRE) mutations cause APECED / APS-1, presenting with candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease.

options.text: Endoplasmic reticulum chaperone promoting correct folding of multi-pass transmembrane receptors
options.explanation: Chaperone defects do not coordinate DNA damage checkpoints or cause extreme radiation hypersensitivity and elevated AFP.

subject: Immunology
topic: Chronic Granulomatous Disease NADPH Oxidase and Catalase-Positive Pathogens
stem: A 3-year-old boy presents with high fever, right upper quadrant abdominal pain, and hepatomegaly. Contrast-enhanced CT reveals a 4-cm multiloculated hepatic abscess, and blood and purulent aspirate cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. His medical history is notable for recurrent cervical lymphadenitis caused by Serratia marcescens at age 14 months and Aspergillus fumigatus pneumonia at age 2 years. Flow cytometry using dihydrorhodamine 123 (DHR) fails to demonstrate any increase in green fluorescence following stimulation of the patient's neutrophils with phorbol myristate acetate (PMA). Nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) dye reduction assay also remains completely negative (colorless). Which of the following biochemical reactions is defective in this patient's phagocytes?

options.text: Oxidation of chloride ions to hypochlorous acid by neutrophil myeloperoxidase in azurophilic granules
options.explanation: Myeloperoxidase (MPO) deficiency impairs HOCl generation, but the respiratory burst itself is intact, so DHR and NBT tests are completely NORMAL.

options.text: Reduction of hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen by endogenous macrophage catalase
options.explanation: Host catalase breaks down H2O2; its absence does not cause CGD (bacterial catalase destroys bacterial H2O2, which prevents host killing).

options.text: Conversion of molecular oxygen to superoxide anion by the phagocytic NADPH oxidase complex
options.explanation: CHRONIC GRANULOMATOUS DISEASE (CGD) is an inborn error of phagocyte microbicidal function, most commonly inherited as an X-LINKED RECESSIVE defect in CYBB encoding gp91phox (the catalytic beta subunit of cytochrome b558 in the NADPH OXIDASE complex). NADPH oxidase transfers electrons from NADPH to molecular oxygen (O2) to generate SUPEROXIDE ANIONS (O2-), initiating the respiratory burst that subsequently yields hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and hypochlorous acid (HOCl via myeloperoxidase). When infected with catalase-negative organisms, phagocytes can utilize bacterial-derived H2O2 to generate microbicidal HOCl. However, CATALASE-POSITIVE ORGANISMS (Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus) destroy their own H2O2, leaving CGD phagocytes powerless to kill them, provoking granuloma formation and recurrent abscesses.

options.text: Degradation of microbial peptidoglycan by primary lysosomal acid hydrolases
options.explanation: Lysosomal acid hydrolase defects cause lysosomal storage diseases (e.g., Gaucher, Tay-Sachs), not CGD.

options.text: Generation of nitric oxide from L-arginine by inducible nitric oxide synthase
options.explanation: iNOS generates nitric oxide to form reactive nitrogen species; it does not generate the superoxide anion measured by DHR or NBT.

topic: Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type 1 CD18 Beta-2 Integrin Extravasation Defect
stem: A 3-week-old male infant is brought to the pediatric hospitalist because his umbilical cord stump has failed to separate. Physical examination reveals an intact, dry umbilical cord stump surrounded by an erythematous abdominal wall without purulent drainage. Two days later, he develops severe, necrotic omphalitis and peritonitis. Complete blood count reveals marked leukocytosis with an absolute neutrophil count of 68,000/uL (normal 2,000-8,000/uL). Despite this massive peripheral neutrophilia, biopsy of the inflamed necrotic periumbilical subcutaneous tissue demonstrates complete absence of neutrophils in the extravascular space. Flow cytometry confirms absent leukocyte cell-surface expression of CD18. Which of the following steps of leukocyte extravasation is directly defective in this patient?

options.text: Low-affinity initial leukocyte rolling along post-capillary venules mediated by P-selectin and E-selectin
options.explanation: Leukocyte rolling is mediated by selectins interacting with carbohydrate ligands (Sialyl Lewis X); defects in Sialyl Lewis X cause LAD Type 2.

options.text: Transendothelial diapedesis mediated by homophilic platelet-endothelial cell adhesion molecule-1 (PECAM-1) binding
options.explanation: PECAM-1 (CD31) mediates the subsequent transendothelial diapedesis step between endothelial junctions, downstream of integrin-mediated tight arrest.

options.text: Directional migration through tissue along a chemical gradient mediated by formyl-peptide and C5a receptors
options.explanation: Chemotaxis occurs after extravasation; in LAD-1, neutrophils cannot leave the intravascular space due to lack of firm adhesion.

options.text: Firm adhesion and arrest on vascular endothelium mediated by beta-2 integrin binding to ICAM-1
options.explanation: LEUKOCYTE ADHESION DEFICIENCY TYPE 1 (LAD-1) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ITGB2 gene on chromosome 21q22.3, which encodes the CD18 (BETA-2 INTEGRIN) COMMON SUBUNIT. CD18 heterodimerizes with CD11a (to form LFA-1), CD11b (Mac-1 / CR3), and CD11c to create functional beta-2 integrins on leukocytes. During leukocyte extravasation: (1) Selectins mediate initial marginal rolling (defective in LAD-2 due to absence of Sialyl Lewis X); (2) Chemokines trigger high-affinity integrin conformational activation; and (3) BETA-2 INTEGRINS BIND TO ICAM-1 (CD54) on activated endothelium, mediating TIGHT ADHESION AND ARREST. In LAD-1, neutrophils roll normally but CANNOT FIRMLY ADHERE OR EXTRAVASATE into infected tissues. Consequently, patients present with: (1) DELAYED UMBILICAL CORD SEPARATION (> 30 days), (2) MARKED PERIPHERAL NEUTROPHILIA, and (3) RECURRENT NECROTIC INFECTIONS WITH ABSENCE OF PUS (NO NEUTROPHILS IN TISSUE).

options.text: Intraphagosomal microbial killing mediated by oxygen-dependent myeloperoxidase catalysis
options.explanation: Microbial killing occurs after phagocytosis; LAD-1 neutrophils have normal respiratory burst and killing capacity if they reach the target.

subject: Immunology
topic: Chediak-Higashi Syndrome LYST Lysosomal Trafficking Giant Azurophilic Granules
stem: A 2-year-old boy presents with high fever, recurrent cutaneous staphylococcal furunculosis, and progressive peripheral sensory neuropathy. Physical examination reveals fair skin, silvery-metallic sheen to his blonde hair, light blue irides, and horizontal nystagmus (partial oculocutaneous albinism). Complete blood count reveals mild neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, and anemia. Peripheral blood smear examination reveals giant, round, peroxidase-positive azurophilic granules within the cytoplasm of neutrophils, eosinophils, and lymphocytes. Diagnostic genetic sequencing confirms an autosomal recessive mutation in the LYST (CHS1) gene. Which of the following cellular processes is defective in this disorder?

options.text: Phagosomal acidification mediated by vacuolar-type H+-ATPase proton pumps
options.explanation: Vacuolar H+-ATPase acidifies lysosomes; its isolated defect does not cause giant fused granules or oculocutaneous albinism.

options.text: Superoxide generation by the membrane-bound cytochrome b558 electron transport chain
options.explanation: Cytochrome b558 defect causes Chronic Granulomatous Disease, which has normal granule size and morphology on peripheral blood smear.

options.text: Polymerization of globular actin into filamentous networks at the leading edge of migrating cells
options.explanation: Actin polymerization defect causes Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome (WASp mutation), characterized by microthrombocytopenia and eczema, not giant granules.

options.text: Post-translational mannose-6-phosphate tagging of lysosomal hydrolases in the cis-Golgi network
options.explanation: Mannose-6-phosphate tagging defect causes I-cell disease (GlcNAc phosphotransferase defect), causing coarse facies and skeletal dysostosis.

options.text: Endosomal and lysosomal vesicle trafficking, fusion, and exocytosis in granulated cells
options.explanation: CHEDIAK-HIGASHI SYNDROME is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in the LYST GENE (lysosomal trafficking regulator). The LYST protein regulates intracellular vesicle docking, membrane fusion, and fission. Defective LYST leads to unregulated, pathological membrane fusion of primary lysosomes, forming GIANT, ABNORMAL LYSOSOMES AND AZUROPHILIC GRANULES in all granulated cells. The multisystem clinical manifestations reflect this transport defect: (1) Giant granules in neutrophils cannot dock or fuse with phagosomes to form phagolysosomes, causing IMPAIRED MICROBICIDAL KILLING and recurrent pyogenic infections; (2) Inability of melanocytes to transfer melanin-containing melanosomes to keratinocytes causes PARTIAL OCULOCUTANEOUS ALBINISM (silvery hair, photophobia); (3) Defective platelet dense granules causes bleeding diathesis; and (4) Impaired neuronal axonal transport causes PROGRESSIVE PERIPHERAL NEUROPATHY.

subject: Immunology
topic: Hyper-IgE Job Syndrome STAT3 Defect and TH17 Lineage Differentiation
stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with severe, chronic pruriginous eczematoid dermatitis, coarse facial features with a prominent forehead and broad nasal bridge, and multiple painless, non-erythematous fluctuant skin abscesses ('cold abscesses') on his scalp and trunk that yield abundant Staphylococcus aureus on aspiration. His dental examination reveals two complete rows of teeth due to failure of primary tooth exfoliation (retained deciduous teeth). He has a history of recurrent S. aureus pneumonias that resolved leaving residual thin-walled, air-filled cavities (pneumatoceles). Laboratory evaluation reveals: absolute neutrophil count normal, serum IgE markedly elevated at 8,400 IU/mL (normal < 100 IU/mL), and normal serum IgG, IgA, and IgM. In vitro T-cell differentiation assays demonstrate failure of naive CD4+ T cells to differentiate into IL-17-producing helper T cells (TH17). Which of the following transcription factors is mutated in this autosomal dominant disorder?

options.text: Signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3) carrying dominant-negative mutations
options.explanation: AUTOSOMAL DOMINANT HYPER-IgE SYNDROME (JOB SYNDROME) is caused by dominant-negative mutations in the STAT3 GENE on chromosome 17q21. STAT3 is the critical transcription factor downstream of IL-6, IL-21, and IL-23 signaling required to differentiate naive CD4+ T cells into T-HELPER 17 (TH17) CELLS. TH17 cells secrete IL-17 and IL-22, which stimulate epithelial cells to produce antimicrobial peptides (beta-defensins) and secrete G-CSF and CXCL8 to RECRUIT NEUTROPHILS to cutaneous and mucosal surfaces. Defective TH17 differentiation impairs neutrophil recruitment, explaining the lack of classic inflammatory warmth and erythema in cutaneous infections ('COLD STAPHYLOCOCCAL ABSCESSES'). Clinical hallmarks include: (1) Severe eczema, (2) 'Cold' staph abscesses, (3) Recurrent pneumonias with PNEUMATOCELES, (4) Coarse facies with retained primary teeth, and (5) ASTRONOMICALLY ELEVATED SERUM IgE.

options.text: Forkhead box protein P3 (FOXP3) carrying loss-of-function missense mutations
options.explanation: FOXP3 mutations cause IPEX syndrome (Immune dysregulation, Polyendocrinopathy, Enteropathy, X-linked) due to absence of regulatory T (Treg) cells, presenting with neonatal type 1 diabetes and severe diarrhea.

options.text: Autoimmune regulator (AIRE) zinc-finger transcription factor
options.explanation: AIRE mutations cause Autoimmune Polyendocrinopathy-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED / APS-1), characterized by chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis and hypoparathyroidism.

options.text: T-box expressed in T cells (T-bet) driving interferon-gamma expression
options.explanation: T-bet is the master transcription factor for TH1 differentiation; its deficiency impairs cell-mediated immunity against mycobacteria, not Job syndrome.

options.text: GATA-binding protein 3 (GATA3) driving interleukin-4 and interleukin-5 expression
options.explanation: GATA3 is the master transcription factor for TH2 differentiation; haploinsufficiency causes HDR syndrome (hypoparathyroidism, deafness, renal dysplasia).

subject: Immunology
topic: Terminal Complement C5-C9 Deficiency and Invasive Neisseria Susceptibility
stem: A 19-year-old college student presents with high fever, severe headache, photophobia, and a petechial rash over his lower extremities. Lumbar puncture demonstrates turbid CSF with 4,200 white blood cells/uL (94% neutrophils), elevated protein, decreased glucose, and Gram-negative kidney bean-shaped intracellular diplococci on Gram stain, confirmed as Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B. He has a documented history of Neisseria meningitidis bacteremia at age 14 and disseminated gonococcal infection at age 17. Serum complement analysis demonstrates completely normal total hemolytic classical complement activity (CH50) and normal alternative pathway activity (AH50), but a specialized assay for terminal complement complex assembly shows 0% functional activity. Flow cytometry confirms normal cell-surface expression of CD55 and CD59. Which of the following complement proteins is most likely deficient in this patient?

options.text: Complement component C1q or C1s (classical pathway initiation components)
options.explanation: Early classical complement deficiencies (C1, C2, C4) impair immune complex clearance, strongly predisposing to Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) and encapsulated pyogenic infections, not isolated Neisserial vulnerability.

options.text: Complement component C7, C8, or C9 (terminal membrane attack complex components)
options.explanation: DEFICIENCIES OF TERMINAL COMPLEMENT COMPONENTS (C5, C6, C7, C8, or C9) prevent the assembly of the MEMBRANE ATTACK COMPLEX (MAC / C5b-9). MAC forms a 10-nanometer transmembrane pore in the outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria, dissipating the proton motive gradient and provoking osmotic lysis. While thick-peptidoglycan Gram-positive bacteria and encapsulated organisms are readily cleared by C3b-mediated opsonization and phagocytosis, NEISSERIA SPECIES (Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae) have thin cell walls with lipooligosaccharide (LOS) and are UNIQUELY DEPENDENT ON MAC-MEDIATED LYSIS for effective host defense. Patients with terminal complement deficiencies have a 1,000- to 10,000-fold increased risk of recurrent invasive Neisserial infections, but have normal immunity against other pyogenic bacteria.

options.text: Complement component C3 (central convertase substrate)
options.explanation: C3 deficiency impairs both opsonization and MAC assembly, predisposing to recurrent life-threatening infections with all pyogenic encapsulated bacteria (Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae) and severe membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis.

options.text: Alternative pathway Factor D or Properdin (alternative convertase stabilizers)
options.explanation: Properdin deficiency is X-linked and predisposes to meningococcal disease, but causes a profoundly abnormal alternative pathway (AH50) assay, whereas this patient has a normal AH50 with an isolated terminal MAC defect.

options.text: Mannose-binding lectin-associated serine protease 2 (MASP-2)
options.explanation: MASP-2 deficiency impairs the lectin complement activation pathway, which typically causes mild or asymptomatic vulnerability to respiratory tract infections.

subject: Immunology
topic: Hereditary Angioedema C1 Inhibitor Deficiency Bradykinin and Kallikrein Axis
stem: A 26-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with severe, painless swelling of her lips, tongue, and face that began 6 hours after a routine dental extraction. Over the past hour, she has developed inspiratory stridor and severe crampy abdominal pain with vomiting. She has experienced similar episodes of facial and limb swelling since adolescence, typically triggered by minor trauma or emotional stress. Physical examination reveals tense, non-pitting edema of the face and oropharynx without urticaria, pruritus, or wheezing. Her blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. Epinephrine, diphenhydramine, and methylprednisolone are administered immediately, but produce ZERO clinical improvement. Serum laboratory evaluation reveals normal serum tryptase, normal C1q, but markedly decreased serum C4 (4 mg/dL, normal 15-45 mg/dL) and low functional C1 inhibitor (C1-INH) activity. Which of the following vasoactive mediators is the direct driver of mucosal and subcutaneous edema in this disorder?

options.text: Histamine released from mast cell granules via IgE-dependent Fc-epsilon-RI cross-linking
options.explanation: Histamine-mediated angioedema is an allergic (type I) response characterized by urticaria, pruritus, and rapid response to epinephrine and antihistamines, unlike HAE.

options.text: Prostaglandin D2 synthesized by activated mucosal eosinophils via cyclooxygenase-2
options.explanation: Prostaglandin D2 participates in allergic asthma and mast cell activation; it does not drive hereditary C1-INH deficiency angioedema.

options.text: Bradykinin generated by unchecked plasma kallikrein cleavage of high-molecular-weight kininogen
options.explanation: HEREDITARY ANGIOEDEMA (HAE) is an autosomal dominant condition caused by deficiency (Type I, 85%) or dysfunction (Type II, 15%) of C1 INHIBITOR (C1-INH, encoded by SERPING1). C1-INH is a serine protease inhibitor (serpin) that physiological regulates two distinct cascades: (1) The complement classical pathway (inhibiting C1r and C1s; unchecked C1s cleaves C4 and C2, explaining the chronically LOW SERUM C4 that serves as the best screening test); and (2) The KALLIKREIN-KININ SYSTEM (inhibiting activated factor XII and plasma kallikrein). Unchecked kallikrein cleaves high-molecular-weight kininogen (HMWK) to liberate massive amounts of BRADYKININ. Bradykinin acts on endothelial B2 receptors, driving vascular permeability and angioedema. Because this process is kinin-mediated rather than histamine-mediated, it manifests WITHOUT URTICARIA OR PRURITUS and is COMPLETELY REFRACTORY TO EPINEPHRINE, ANTIHISTAMINES, AND CORTICOSTEROIDS.

options.text: Leukotriene C4 and D4 generated by 5-lipoxygenase in basophils
options.explanation: Cysteinyl leukotrienes mediate bronchoconstriction and vascular permeability in asthma and anaphylaxis; they do not mediate HAE.

options.text: Tumor necrosis factor-alpha released from tissue-resident dendritic cells
options.explanation: TNF-alpha is a pro-inflammatory cytokine driving fever, acute-phase reactants, and septic shock, not acute paroxysmal kinin-mediated angioedema.

topic: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria PIGA Mutation and GPI Anchor CD55/CD59
stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with severe fatigue, episodic dark red-brown morning urine, and acute, severe right upper quadrant pain. Abdominal Doppler ultrasound demonstrates acute thrombosis of the hepatic veins and inferior vena cava (Budd-Chiari syndrome). Laboratory evaluation reveals: hemoglobin 7.8 g/dL, reticulocytes 9.2%, haptoglobin undetectable (< 5 mg/dL), lactate dehydrogenase markedly elevated at 2,850 U/L (normal < 250 U/L), and negative direct and indirect antiglobulin (Coombs) tests. Urinalysis demonstrates heavy hemosiderinuria. Flow cytometry of peripheral blood erythrocytes and granulocytes confirms the absence of glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchored proteins (GPI-APs). Which of the following regulatory proteins is normally anchored by GPI and directly prevents assembly of the terminal membrane attack complex on autologous erythrocytes?

options.text: CD46 (membrane cofactor protein / MCP mediating factor I cleavage)
options.explanation: CD46 (MCP) is a transmembrane glycoprotein, not a GPI-anchored protein; its expression is normal in PNH.

options.text: Complement receptor 1 (CR1 / CD35) on erythrocyte membranes
options.explanation: CR1 is an integral transmembrane protein that binds C3b/C4b to transport immune complexes; it is not anchored via a GPI linkage.

options.text: Factor H circulating fluid-phase complement regulatory glycoprotein
options.explanation: Factor H is a soluble plasma glycoprotein produced by the liver, not a cell-surface GPI-anchored membrane protein.

options.text: CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis / MAC-inhibitory protein)
options.explanation: PAROXYSMAL NOCTURNAL HEMOGLOBINURIA (PNH) is an acquired clonal hematopoietic stem cell disorder caused by a somatic mutation in the X-linked PIGA GENE (phosphatidylinositol glycan class A). PIGA is essential for the first step in the biosynthesis of GLYCOSYLPHOSPHATIDYLINOSITOL (GPI) ANCHORS, which tether proteins to cell membranes. PNH cells lack all GPI-anchored proteins, including two critical complement-regulatory proteins: (1) CD55 (Decay-Accelerating Factor / DAF), which accelerates the dissociation of C3 and C5 convertases; and (2) CD59 (MAC-INHIBITORY PROTEIN / MIRL), which directly binds C8 and C9, preventing the polymerization of C9 into the TERMINAL MEMBRANE ATTACK COMPLEX (MAC). Absence of CD59 permits unregulated, spontaneous complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis (exacerbated at night during mild respiratory acidosis). Hemoglobinuria, nitric oxide depletion (causing smooth muscle spasm, dysphagia, erectile dysfunction), and life-threatening VENOUS THROMBOSIS (Budd-Chiari syndrome) characterize PNH.

options.text: Vitronectin (S-protein) binding soluble C5b-7 complexes in plasma
options.explanation: Vitronectin is a circulating plasma protein that prevents insertion of fluid-phase terminal complement complexes, not a cellular GPI-anchored protein.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Duffy Blood Group Antigen Receptor and Plasmodium Vivax Resistance
stem: An epidemiological survey in West and Central Africa reveals that over 95% of the indigenous population exhibits natural resistance to blood-stage infection with Plasmodium vivax, despite frequent exposure to the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes. In contrast, infection rates with Plasmodium falciparum remain exceptionally high in the same geographic region. Genetic analysis demonstrates that resistant individuals carry a homozygous promoter mutation (c.-67T>C in the GATA-1 binding box) of the ACKR1 gene encoding the Duffy antigen receptor for chemokines (DARC), resulting in a null Fy(a-b-) phenotype on erythrocytes while preserving endothelial expression. Which of the following biological processes explains this selective resistance to Plasmodium vivax?

options.text: Duffy-negative erythrocytes possess enhanced intracellular levels of reduced glutathione that kill ingested trophozoites
options.explanation: Glutathione enhances parasite survival; G6PD deficiency impairs glutathione and confers resistance, but Duffy resistance is purely an entry-receptor block.

options.text: The Duffy glycoprotein serves as an obligatory channel for intraerythrocytic export of parasite-derived hemozoin pigment
options.explanation: Hemozoin is formed by parasite biocrystallization of toxic heme within its food vacuole, not exported through erythrocyte Duffy channels.

options.text: DARC expression is required for surface display of PfEMP-1 mediating microvascular endothelial cytoadherence
options.explanation: PfEMP-1 is expressed exclusively by Plasmodium FALCIPARUM and mediates cytoadherence via CD36 and ICAM-1, not P. vivax.

options.text: Absence of the Duffy antigen stimulates pre-erythrocytic complement-mediated lysis of sporozoites in the liver
options.explanation: DARC is expressed on erythrocytes, not hepatocytes; Duffy-negative individuals are fully infected by sporozoites in the liver, but the merozoites cannot enter red cells.

options.text: Merozoite surface Duffy-binding protein (PvDBP) requires the erythrocyte Duffy glycoprotein for junction formation and red cell invasion
options.explanation: PLASMODIUM VIVAX (and Plasmodium knowlesi) merozoites require interaction with the erythrocyte DUFFY ANTIGEN RECEPTOR FOR CHEMOKINES (DARC / ACKR1 / CD234) to successfully invade human red blood cells. The merozoite secretes DUFFY-BINDING PROTEIN (PvDBP) from its micronemes, which binds with high affinity to the extracellular N-terminal domain of the Duffy glycoprotein, establishing an irreversible junction required for actin-myosin-driven invasion. Individuals who are DUFFY-NEGATIVE (Fy[a-b-]), highly prevalent in sub-Saharan and West Africa due to a protective GATA-box promoter mutation, lack DARC on erythrocyte surfaces. Consequently, P. vivax merozoites cannot bind or penetrate red blood cells, rendering these individuals COMPLETELY RESISTANT TO P. VIVAX MALARIA. In contrast, Plasmodium falciparum uses multiple redundant alternative receptors (glycophorins A, B, C) and readily invades Duffy-negative cells.

subject: Microbiology
topic: CCR5 Delta-32 Mutation and HIV-1 Coreceptor Binding Resistance
stem: A 32-year-old hemophilia patient who received repeated unheated factor VIII concentrates in the early 1980s from donors subsequently confirmed to have died of AIDS remains persistently seronegative for HIV-1 antibodies and has undetectable plasma HIV-1 RNA on repeated testing. In vitro infection assays demonstrate that his isolated peripheral blood CD4+ T lymphocytes and macrophages are completely resistant to infection by primary viral isolates of R5 (macrophage-tropic) HIV-1, but remain susceptible to laboratory-adapted X4 (T-cell-tropic) strains. Genetic sequencing of the patient's chemokine receptor genes reveals a homozygous 32-base-pair deletion in the CCR5 gene (CCR5-delta-32). Which of the following viral glycoproteins normally interacts with this host coreceptor to mediate viral membrane fusion?

options.text: Viral surface envelope glycoprotein gp120 following conformational change induced by CD4 binding
options.explanation: HIV-1 entry into host target cells is a multi-step process: (1) The VIRAL SURFACE GLYCOPROTEIN gp120 binds to the primary host receptor, CD4; (2) CD4 binding induces a critical conformational change in gp120 that exposes a conserved coreceptor-binding loop; (3) gp120 binds to a host 7-transmembrane CHEMOKINE CORECEPTOR: either CCR5 (predominant in early transmission; macrophage-tropic / R5 viruses) or CXCR4 (predominant in late disease; T-cell-tropic / X4 viruses); (4) Coreceptor engagement triggers insertion of the hydrophobic fusion peptide of the TRANSMEMBRANE GLYCOPROTEIN gp41 into the host cell membrane, driving viral and host membrane fusion. Individuals homozygous for the CCR5-delta-32 DELETION produce a truncated, non-functional receptor that never reaches the cell surface, conferring nearly complete RESISTANCE TO INFECTION BY R5 HIV-1 STRAINS.

options.text: Viral transmembrane glycoprotein gp41 binding directly to the chemokine receptor before CD4 contact
options.explanation: gp41 mediates membrane fusion after coreceptor binding; it does not bind CCR5 directly, and CD4 binding is an obligatory initial requirement.

options.text: Capsid protein p24 interacting with cytoplasmic host cyclophilin A during uncoating
options.explanation: p24 forms the viral conical capsid and interacts with cyclophilin A during uncoating; it has no role in initial cell-surface receptor binding.

options.text: Matrix protein p17 binding to host membrane phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate
options.explanation: p17 forms the inner matrix shell of the viral envelope and aids nuclear import; it does not bind external chemokine coreceptors.

options.text: Viral accessory protein Nef down-regulating host cell-surface MHC class I molecules
options.explanation: Nef down-regulates CD4 and MHC class I to evade cytotoxic T cells; it does not mediate viral attachment or coreceptor entry.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Epstein-Barr Virus Latency Membrane Protein 1 and CD40 Molecular Mimicry
stem: A 10-year-old boy from equatorial East Africa presents with a rapidly expanding, painless, massive destructive mass of his right mandible. Biopsy of the mass reveals sheets of uniform, medium-sized lymphoid cells with round nuclei, coarsely clumped chromatin, and multiple nucleoli, interspersed with benign tingible-body macrophages containing apoptotic cellular debris, producing a characteristic 'starry-sky' histological appearance. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) confirms a t(8;14)(q24;q32) chromosomal translocation. In vitro molecular virology studies demonstrate that Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infects B cells and immortalizes them through the expression of Latent Membrane Protein 1 (LMP1). Which of the following host immune receptors is constitutively mimicked by LMP1 to drive continuous B-cell proliferation and survival?

options.text: Interleukin-2 receptor alpha chain (CD25) stimulating constitutive JAK-STAT3 phosphorylation
options.explanation: CD25 is the high-affinity IL-2 receptor alpha subunit upregulated on activated T cells, not the target mimicked by EBV LMP1 in B cells.

options.text: CD40 receptor acting through TNF receptor-associated factors (TRAFs) to constitutively activate NF-kappa-B and MAPK
options.explanation: EPSTEIN-BARR VIRUS (EBV) drives B-cell transformation and immortalization primarily via LATENT MEMBRANE PROTEIN 1 (LMP1). LMP1 functions as a CONSTITUTIVELY ACTIVE MOLECULAR MIMIC OF CD40. In normal B cells, CD40 requires binding to CD40L (CD154) on helper T cells to induce oligomerization. In contrast, LMP1 self-aggregates in the host plasma membrane independently of any ligand. Its cytoplasmic C-terminal activation regions (CTAR1 and CTAR2) recruit TNF RECEPTOR-ASSOCIATED FACTORS (TRAFs), constitutively activating the NF-KAPPA-B, JNK/AP-1, and MAPK pathways. This upregulates anti-apoptotic proteins (BCL-2, Mcl-1) and stimulates cell-cycle entry, driving clonal B-cell expansion. In endemic Burkitt lymphoma, malaria-induced immunosuppression permits uncontrolled expansion of EBV-infected B cells, dramatically increasing the likelihood of an erroneous AID-mediated t(8;14) MYC-IgH translocation.

options.text: B-cell receptor (surface IgM) activating spleen tyrosine kinase (Syk) and Bruton tyrosine kinase
options.explanation: EBV Latent Membrane Protein 2A (LMP2A) mimics the B-cell receptor (providing survival signals without antigen), whereas LMP1 mimics CD40.

options.text: Fas receptor (CD95) recruiting Fas-associated death domain (FADD) proteins
options.explanation: Fas engagement triggers caspase activation and apoptosis; LMP1 promotes survival by inhibiting apoptosis through NF-kappa-B.

options.text: Chemokine receptor CXCR4 driving directed homing to bone marrow stromal cell-derived factor-1
options.explanation: CXCR4 regulates lymphocyte homing and metastasis, not the constitutive proliferative costimulatory signal mimicked by LMP1.

subject: Pharmacology
topic: Cytomegalovirus UL97 Kinase Ganciclovir Monophosphorylation and Resistance
stem: A 44-year-old man with end-stage renal disease undergoes deceased-donor renal transplantation. Three months later, while receiving immunosuppressive therapy with tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and prednisone, he develops high fever, leukopenia, and worsening graft dysfunction. Quantitative PCR demonstrates a high cytomegalovirus (CMV) viral load of 850,000 copies/mL. Intravenous ganciclovir therapy is initiated. Cellular pharmacology analysis demonstrates that ganciclovir is an acyclic nucleoside analogue of 2'-deoxyguanosine that requires three sequential phosphorylation steps to become active: the initial, rate-limiting monophosphorylation is catalyzed by a viral protein kinase, followed by di- and triphosphorylation by host cellular kinases. Which of the following viral gene products catalyzes this essential initial monophosphorylation of ganciclovir in CMV-infected cells?

options.text: Viral thymidine kinase encoded by the UL23 gene locus
options.explanation: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella-zoster virus (VZV) encode thymidine kinase (TK) to monophosphorylate acyclovir and ganciclovir; CMV lacks thymidine kinase entirely.

options.text: Viral DNA-dependent DNA polymerase encoded by the UL54 gene
options.explanation: UL54 encodes CMV DNA polymerase, which is the downstream target inhibited by ganciclovir triphosphate, not the monophosphorylating kinase.

options.text: UL97 viral serine/threonine protein kinase (phosphotransferase)
options.explanation: GANCICLOVIR is a guanosine analogue prodrug used for cytomegalovirus (CMV) infections. To inhibit viral replication, ganciclovir must be converted intracellularly to its active form, ganciclovir triphosphate. Crucially, human cytomegalovirus (unlike HSV and VZV) DOES NOT ENCODE A THYMIDINE KINASE. Instead, the rate-limiting initial monophosphorylation of ganciclovir in CMV-infected cells is catalyzed by the VIRAL UL97 SERINE/THREONINE KINASE (phosphotransferase). Once monophosphorylated, host cellular kinases convert it to ganciclovir triphosphate, which competitively inhibits viral DNA polymerase (UL54) and terminates DNA chain elongation. Mutations in the UL97 GENE (e.g., M460V, H520Q, C592G) prevent ganciclovir monophosphorylation and are the primary cause of GANCICLOVIR RESISTANCE in clinical practice.

options.text: Viral ribonucleotide reductase large catalytic subunit
options.explanation: Ribonucleotide reductase converts ribonucleotides to deoxyribonucleotides; it is not the kinase responsible for ganciclovir activation.

options.text: Viral major capsid protein assembly protease encoded by UL80
options.explanation: UL80 is a maturational protease that cleaves the viral scaffold protein during capsid assembly, with no kinase activity.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Hepatitis B Virus Reverse Transcription of Pregenomic RNA and cccDNA
stem: An investigator studies the replication cycle of hepatitis B virus (HBV) in primary human hepatocyte cultures. After the enveloped virion enters the hepatocyte via the sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP) receptor, the partially double-stranded relaxed circular DNA (rcDNA) genome is released into the cytoplasm and transported to the nucleus. Inside the nucleus, host cellular repair enzymes convert rcDNA into covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), which forms a stable viral minichromosome. Cellular RNA polymerase II then transcribes cccDNA into several viral mRNAs, including a greater-than-genome-length transcript known as pregenomic RNA (pgRNA). Which of the following enzymatic events occurs inside the newly assembled viral nucleocapsid in the cytoplasm to generate new viral genomic DNA?

options.text: Host cellular DNA polymerase alpha replicates both strands simultaneously via semi-conservative leading and lagging strand synthesis
options.explanation: HBV does not replicate via host DNA polymerase; its genome is replicated by its own viral reverse transcriptase inside cytoplasmic capsids.

options.text: Viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase replicates pregenomic RNA into double-stranded RNA replication intermediates
options.explanation: Replication via an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase producing dsRNA intermediates is characteristic of RNA viruses (e.g., Reoviridae, Coronaviridae), not HBV.

options.text: Host topoisomerase II cleaves cccDNA into linear fragments that integrate into the host genome to initiate rolling-circle DNA replication
options.explanation: HBV does not require integration for viral replication (cccDNA acts as the template), and it does not use rolling-circle replication.

options.text: Viral reverse transcriptase copies pregenomic RNA into negative-strand DNA and subsequently synthesizes partial positive-strand DNA
options.explanation: HEPATITIS B VIRUS (Hepadnaviridae) is a unique partially double-stranded DNA virus that replicates through an RNA INTERMEDIATE via REVERSE TRANSCRIPTION. In the hepatocyte nucleus, host DNA repair enzymes convert relaxed circular DNA (rcDNA) into COVALENTLY CLOSED CIRCULAR DNA (cccDNA), which persists indefinitely as an episomal minichromosome. Host RNA polymerase II transcribes cccDNA into PREGENOMIC RNA (pgRNA). pgRNA is packaged into assembling capsids in the cytoplasm along with the VIRAL DNA POLYMERASE (which possesses reverse transcriptase, RNA-dependent DNA polymerase, and RNase H activities). Inside the capsid, the polymerase reverse-transcribes pgRNA into a FULL-LENGTH COMPLEMENTARY NEGATIVE-STRAND DNA, degrades the pgRNA template via RNase H, and then uses a leftover RNA primer to synthesize a PARTIAL POSITIVE-STRAND DNA, yielding mature rcDNA.

options.text: Viral integrase inserts the linear double-stranded DNA copy into transcriptionally active host chromosomal loci
options.explanation: Retroviruses (e.g., HIV) require integrase to integrate proviral DNA into host chromosomes; HBV does not encode an integrase and does not require integration for virion assembly.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Hepatitis D Virus Subviral Satellite Dependence on HBsAg Envelope Coating
stem: A 36-year-old man who is a chronic carrier of hepatitis B virus (HBsAg positive for 8 years, HBeAg negative, anti-HBe positive, with normal ALT) presents with acute jaundice, dark urine, and severe fatigue. Laboratory evaluation reveals an acute dramatic spike in serum ALT to 2,140 U/L and total bilirubin to 8.2 mg/dL. Serological testing reveals newly positive anti-HDV IgM and detectable HDV RNA. Liver biopsy demonstrates severe acute lobular necroinflammatory activity with eosinophilic hepatocellular degeneration. Molecular virology confirms that hepatitis D virus (HDV) is a defective single-stranded circular negative-sense RNA subviral agent that cannot complete its life cycle or cause secondary infection in the absence of helper virus functions. Which of the following specific structural components must be provided by hepatitis B virus to enable HDV virion assembly, envelope coating, and subsequent hepatocyte entry?

options.text: Hepatitis B core antigen (HBcAg) forming the icosahedral nucleocapsid shell
options.explanation: HDV packages its circular RNA inside its own Hepatitis Delta Antigen (HDAg), not HBcAg; it utilizes only HBsAg for its outer coat.

options.text: Hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg) functioning as an extracellular immunosuppressive decoy
options.explanation: HBeAg is a secreted non-structural protein derived from precore/core processing; it is not incorporated into HDV virions.

options.text: Hepatitis B viral reverse transcriptase providing RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity
options.explanation: HDV replicates its RNA genome using host cellular RNA polymerase II, which acts as an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase; it does not use HBV reverse transcriptase.

options.text: Hepatitis B X protein (HBx) transactivating host anti-apoptotic survival pathways
options.explanation: While HBx transactivates viral transcription in HBV, it is not an obligatory structural or enzymatic requirement for HDV packaging.

options.text: Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) proteins forming the outer envelope lipid bilayer
options.explanation: HEPATITIS D VIRUS (HDV / Delta agent) is a DEFECTIVE, replication-incompetent subviral satellite virus. Its genome is a tiny, circular, single-stranded negative-sense RNA that encodes a single structural protein: the HEPATITIS DELTA ANTIGEN (HDAg: small-HDAg for replication, large-HDAg for packaging). HDV has NO GENES FOR ENVELOPE PROTEINS. Inside an infected hepatocyte, HDV RNA replicates autonomously using host RNA polymerase II. However, to assemble mature infectious virions that can bud from the host cell and infect adjacent hepatocytes, HDV STRICTLY REQUIRES THE COATING OF ITS RIBONUCLEOPROTEIN CORE BY HEPATITIS B SURFACE ANTIGEN (HBsAg). Because HBsAg binds the sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP) receptor on human hepatocytes, HDV cannot enter or infect cells without HBsAg.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Human Papillomavirus E6 and E7 Oncoproteins p53 and pRb Inactivation
stem: A 38-year-old woman with a 15-year history of cigarette smoking and inconsistent cervical screening presents with postcoital bleeding and foul-smelling vaginal discharge. Pelvic examination reveals an exophytic, ulcerated, friable mass on the posterior ectocervix measuring 3.5 cm. Cervical punch biopsy confirms invasive squamous cell carcinoma. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing confirms the presence of high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) type 16 DNA integrated into the host genome. Molecular oncogenesis studies demonstrate that high-risk HPV drives malignant transformation via two viral oncoproteins, E6 and E7. Which of the following pairs correctly pairs each viral oncoprotein with its specific host tumor suppressor target and molecular mechanism of inactivation?

options.text: E6 binds E6AP ubiquitin ligase to degrade p53; E7 binds and inactivates pRb, releasing active E2F transcription factors
options.explanation: HIGH-RISK HUMAN PAPILLOMAVIRUSES (HPV types 16, 18, 31, 33) drive cervical, anogenital, and oropharyngeal carcinogenesis through the coordinated action of two viral oncoproteins: (1) E6 ONCOPROTEIN binds to the host ubiquitin ligase E6-ASSOCIATED PROTEIN (E6AP). The E6-E6AP complex binds the tumor suppressor p53, polyubiquitinating it and directing it to the 26S PROTEASOME FOR DEGRADATION. Loss of p53 abolishes DNA-damage cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis. (2) E7 ONCOPROTEIN binds to the hypophosphorylated active form of the RETINOBLASTOMA PROTEIN (pRb). Binding disrupts the pRb-E2F complex, RELEASING FREE E2F TRANSCRIPTION FACTORS that drive transcription of cyclin E, cyclin A, and thymidine kinase, forcing the cell through the G1/S CHECKPOINT into uncontrolled S-phase DNA synthesis.

options.text: E6 phosphorylates pRb causing its nuclear translocation; E7 acts as a direct inhibitor of cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p16
options.explanation: E7 inactivates pRb; inactivation of pRb causes compensatory, marked overexpression of p16 (INK4a), which serves as a clinical biomarker for high-risk HPV.

options.text: E6 cleaves the extracellular domain of epidermal growth factor receptor; E7 binds and degrades p53 via caspases
options.explanation: E6 degrades p53 via the proteasome, not E7; E7 targets pRb.

options.text: E6 inhibits the catalytic subunit of telomerase reverse transcriptase; E7 blocks MYC transcription
options.explanation: E6 actually ACTIVATES telomerase (hTERT) to maintain telomere length; it does not inhibit telomerase.

options.text: E6 binds and sequesters the mismatch repair protein MSH2; E7 cleaves adenomatous polyposis coli (APC)
options.explanation: HPV oncoproteins do not specifically target MSH2 or APC; their classic well-characterized targets are p53 (E6) and pRb (E7).

subject: Microbiology
topic: Parvovirus B19 P Antigen Globoside and Erythroid Progenitor Cytotoxicity
stem: An 8-year-old boy with homozygous sickle cell disease (HbSS) is brought to the emergency department with profound weakness, lethargy, pallor, and dyspnea on minimal exertion. Physical examination reveals an extremely pale, tachycardic child with a systolic ejection murmur, but no splenomegaly. Laboratory evaluation demonstrates an acute drop in hemoglobin from his baseline of 8.6 g/dL to 3.4 g/dL. His reticulocyte count is shockingly depressed at 0.1% (normal for HbSS: 8-15%, absolute reticulocytes < 10,000/uL). Bone marrow aspiration reveals giant proerythroblasts with prominent intranuclear viral inclusion bodies and complete arrest of erythropoiesis, with normal myeloid and megakaryocytic lineages. Serum PCR is positive for Parvovirus B19 DNA. Which of the following host cell-surface molecules acts as the primary receptor for Parvovirus B19 attachment and cellular entry?

options.text: Glycophorin A sialoglycoprotein on mature unnucleated erythrocytes
options.explanation: Glycophorin A is the erythrocyte receptor for Plasmodium falciparum EBA-175 and influenza virus, not Parvovirus B19.

options.text: Blood group P antigen (globoside / tetrahexosylceramide) on erythroid progenitor cells
options.explanation: PARVOVIRUS B19 is a non-enveloped, single-stranded DNA virus (the smallest DNA virus). It exhibits strict tropism for HUMAN ERYTHROID PROGENITOR CELLS (erythroblasts, BFU-E, CFU-E). The primary cellular receptor for Parvovirus B19 attachment is the BLOOD GROUP P ANTIGEN (GLOBOSIDE, a neutral glycosphingolipid). Individuals who lack the P antigen (p phenotype, rare autosomal recessive) are completely resistant to Parvovirus B19 infection. Once bound to globoside, coreceptors (alpha-5-beta-1 integrin) facilitate viral internalization. The non-structural protein 1 (NS1) of the virus arrests host cells in the G2/M phase and triggers apoptosis. In patients with chronic hemolytic anemias (sickle cell, hereditary spherocytosis), destruction of erythroid progenitors causes a temporary complete shutdown of red cell production, resulting in life-threatening APLASTIC CRISIS (marked anemia with RETICULOCYTOPENIA).

options.text: Duffy antigen receptor for chemokines (DARC) on normocytic reticulocytes
options.explanation: DARC is the receptor for Plasmodium vivax merozoite invasion, not Parvovirus B19.

options.text: Transferrin receptor 1 (CD71) mediating endocytosis of ferric iron
options.explanation: CD71 is expressed on erythroid precursors, but Parvovirus B19 attachment is mediated specifically by the P antigen (globoside).

options.text: Erythropoietin receptor coupled to Janus kinase 2 on committed CFU-E cells
options.explanation: Erythropoietin binds the EpoR to stimulate erythropoiesis, but Parvovirus B19 does not bind EpoR for cellular entry.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Clostridioides Difficile Toxins A and B Rho GTPase Glucosylation Mechanism
stem: A 68-year-old woman develops profuse, foul-smelling watery diarrhea (8-10 episodes per day), crampy abdominal pain, fever (38.8 C), and marked leukocytosis (white blood cell count 26,000/uL with 88% neutrophils) 10 days after completing a course of clindamycin for an aspiration pneumonia. Sigmoidoscopy reveals diffuse hyperemic colonic mucosa covered by discrete, punctate, yellowish-white mucosal plaques. Microscopic examination of the plaques reveals inflammatory pseudomembranes composed of fibrin, mucin, necrotic colonic epithelial cells, and dense neutrophil infiltration ('volcano lesions'). Stool PCR is positive for Clostridioides difficile toxin genes. Molecular analysis indicates that C. difficile virulence is mediated by Toxin A (enterotoxin) and Toxin B (cytotoxin). Which of the following biochemical mechanisms accounts for the cytotoxicity and disruption of the intestinal epithelial barrier caused by these toxins?

options.text: ADP-ribosylation of the alpha-subunit of Gs proteins stimulating constitutive adenylyl cyclase activity
options.explanation: ADP-ribosylation of Gs causing constitutive cAMP activation is the mechanism of Vibrio cholerae cholera toxin and ETEC heat-labile toxin (LT).

options.text: Cleavage of the 28S ribosomal RNA of the 60S eukaryotic ribosomal subunit halting translation
options.explanation: Cleaving 28S rRNA to halt translation is the mechanism of Shiga toxin (Shigella dysenteriae) and Shiga-like toxins (EHEC).

options.text: Monoglucosylation of low-molecular-weight Rho-family GTPases (Rho, Rac, Cdc42) using UDP-glucose as a substrate
options.explanation: CLOSTRIDIOIDES DIFFICILE produces two large clostridial glucosylating toxins: TOXIN A (TcdA, enterotoxin) and TOXIN B (TcdB, potent cytotoxin). Both toxins enter colonic enterocytes via receptor-mediated endocytosis, followed by low-pH-induced pore formation and autoproteolytic release of their N-terminal glucosyltransferase catalytic domain into the host cytosol. The toxins catalyze the MONOGLUCOSYLATION OF RHO-FAMILY SMALL GTPases (RhoA, Rac1, and Cdc42) at a conserved threonine residue (Thr-37 in RhoA), utilizing intracellular UDP-GLUCOSE as the sugar donor. Glucosylation permanently locks Rho GTPases in an inactive conformation. Because Rho GTPases control actin dynamics and tight junction assembly, their inactivation triggers: (1) COLLAPSE OF THE ACTIN CYTOSKELETON, (2) LOSS OF TIGHT JUNCTION INTEGRITY (zonula occludens breakdown with severe fluid leak and watery diarrhea), and (3) ENTEROCYTE APOPTOSIS with massive neutrophil recruitment and pseudomembrane formation.

options.text: Proteolytic cleavage of synaptobrevin (VAMP) preventing exocytic neurotransmitter vesicle release
options.explanation: Synaptobrevin cleavage is the mechanism of Clostridium tetani (tetanospasmin) and Clostridium botulinum toxins.

options.text: Lecithinase activity hydrolyzing phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin in cell membranes
options.explanation: Lecithinase (alpha-toxin, phospholipase C) causing gas gangrene is produced by Clostridium perfringens, not C. difficile.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Pseudomonas Aeruginosa Exotoxin A Elongation Factor 2 ADP-Ribosylation
stem: A 42-year-old man with severe extensive third-degree burns covering 45% of his total body surface area is hospitalized in the burn intensive care unit. On hospital day 12, he develops high fevers, worsening tachycardia, hypotension, and green-pigmented, sweet grape-like smelling purulent drainage from his burn wounds. Examination reveals scattered necrotic cutaneous lesions with central black eschar surrounded by an erythematous halo (ecthyma gangrenosum). Blood cultures grow an oxidase-positive, non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative rod that produces a blue-green pyocyanin pigment. The major virulence factor responsible for tissue necrosis in this organism is Exotoxin A. Which of the following biochemical mechanisms describes the enzymatic action of Pseudomonas aeruginosa Exotoxin A inside host cells?

options.text: Ribosomal RNA N-glycosylase activity cleaving a single adenine from the 28S rRNA sarcin-ricin loop
options.explanation: Cleaving adenine from 28S rRNA describes Shiga toxin and ricin, not Pseudomonas Exotoxin A.

options.text: Direct ADP-ribosylation of the inhibitory G-protein alpha-subunit (Gi), locking it in an inactive state
options.explanation: ADP-ribosylation of Gi to prevent adenylyl cyclase inhibition is the mechanism of Bordetella pertussis pertussis toxin.

options.text: Zinc-dependent endopeptidase cleavage of vesicle-associated membrane proteins in motor neurons
options.explanation: Cleavage of synaptobrevin/VAMP is the mechanism of tetanus and botulinum neurotoxins, not Pseudomonas Exotoxin A.

options.text: ADP-ribosylation of diphthamide residues on eukaryotic elongation factor 2 (EF-2), halting protein synthesis
options.explanation: PSEUDOMONAS AERUGINOSA produces multiple virulence factors, but its most potent lethal factor is EXOTOXIN A. Exotoxin A is an AB toxin that binds to the host alpha-2-macroglobulin receptor (LRP1) via its B subunit and undergoes endocytosis. Inside the host cytosol, the catalytic A subunit catalyzes the ADP-RIBOSYLATION OF ELONGATION FACTOR 2 (EF-2). Specifically, it transfers an ADP-ribose moiety from NAD+ onto DIPHTHAMIDE (a post-translationally modified histidine residue unique to EF-2). This covalent modification permanently inactivates EF-2, preventing ribosome translocation and COMPLETELY HALTING HOST CELL PROTEIN SYNTHESIS, leading to rapid cell death and tissue necrosis (as seen in ecthyma gangrenosum). This mechanism is MOLECULARLY IDENTICAL to that of DIPHTHERIA TOXIN produced by Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

options.text: Pore-forming cholesterol-dependent cytolysin disrupting eukaryotic plasma membrane integrity
options.explanation: Pore-forming cytolysins include listeriolysin O and streptolysin O; Pseudomonas Exotoxin A is an intracellular enzyme that inhibits translation.

subject: Microbiology
topic: Corynebacterium Diphtheriae Toxin Heparin-Binding EGF Receptor Entry
stem: A 5-year-old unimmunized girl recently immigrated from an area with low vaccination coverage presents with severe sore throat, fever, hoarseness, and painful bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy producing a prominent 'bull-neck' appearance. Physical examination reveals a thick, leathery, grayish-brown pseudomembrane firmly adherent to the posterior pharyngeal wall, uvula, and bilateral tonsillar pillars. Attempted gentle scraping of the membrane elicits profuse bleeding. 12-lead ECG reveals prolonged PR interval and frequent premature ventricular complexes (myocarditis). Gram stain of pharyngeal swabs demonstrates Gram-positive pleomorphic club-shaped rods arranged in angular V- or L-shaped clumps ('Chinese characters') that stain metachromatic with methylene blue (Albert stain). Which of the following host cell-surface receptors mediates the binding and receptor-mediated endocytosis of the B subunit of diphtheria toxin?

options.text: Low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1 / CD91)
options.explanation: LRP1 is the host receptor for Pseudomonas Exotoxin A, not diphtheria toxin (which uses HB-EGF).

options.text: Ganglioside GM1 on intestinal brush border microvillus membranes
options.explanation: Ganglioside GM1 is the receptor for Vibrio cholerae cholera toxin and E. coli heat-labile enterotoxin.

options.text: Polysialic acid on neural cell adhesion molecules (NCAM)
options.explanation: NCAM polysialic acid mediates neuronal plasticity and cell migration; it does not serve as the diphtheria toxin receptor.

options.text: Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) complexed with myeloid differentiation factor 2
options.explanation: TLR4-MD2 recognizes Gram-negative lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin), not the protein B subunit of diphtheria exotoxin.

options.text: Heparin-binding epidermal growth factor-like precursor (HB-EGF)
options.explanation: CORYNEBACTERIUM DIPHTHERIAE produces DIPHTHERIA TOXIN, an AB exotoxin encoded by the tox gene carried by a temperate lysogenic bacteriophage (CORYNEPHAGE BETA). The toxin is synthesized as a single polypeptide that is cleaved into an A (catalytic) and B (binding) subunit linked by a disulfide bridge. The B SUBUNIT binds specifically to the HEPARIN-BINDING EPIDERMAL GROWTH FACTOR-LIKE PRECURSOR (HB-EGF / pro-HB-EGF), a cell-surface receptor widely expressed on myocardial cells, peripheral nerve Schwann cells, and mucosal epithelium. Receptor engagement triggers receptor-mediated endocytosis. Acidification of the endosome induces a conformational change that translocates the A catalytic subunit into the cytosol, where it ADP-RIBOSYLATES DIPHTHAMIDE ON ELONGATION FACTOR 2 (EF-2), halting protein synthesis. High HB-EGF expression in the myocardium and peripheral nerves explains the lethal complications: TOXIC MYOCARDITIS (conduction block) and NEUROPATHY (cranial nerve palsies, soft palate paralysis).
